cim: Will AI Change North Korea’s Nuclear Calculus? - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
cim_eredeti: Will AI Change North Korea’s Nuclear Calculus? - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
szoveg_eredeti:
Washington has spent years debating the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in nuclear command and control, and agonizing over the military implications of China-U.S. AI competition. It has spent far less time asking a different question: how will North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s deterrence calculus change if he believes the United States is on the verge of obtaining a powerful, enduring advantage in artificial general intelligence?

Artificial general intelligence (AGI) – defined as powerful intelligence matching human performance across cognitive tasks – could further destabilize nuclear deterrence relationships that are already deteriorating. Weaker, non-AGI powers could become especially problematic. North Korea’s nuclear posture is already on a hair trigger. If the United States obtains AGI or AGI-like capabilities, Pyongyang could adopt an aggressive “use it or lose it” mentality because it fears a first strike that eradicates its nuclear weapons capabilities and decapitates its leadership.

Critically, the United States’ actual acquisition of AGI and the subsequent development of deterrence-nullifying capabilities matters less than North Korea’s perceptions of U.S. capabilities and intent. Because Pyongyang has adopted an aggressive nuclear posture and espouses such a critical, paranoid view of U.S. intentions, the situation could spiral even before AGI capabilities are operational. More attention should therefore be paid to how AGI could upset asymmetric deterrence equilibria, especially vis-à-vis Pyongyang.

If AGI takeoff truly unlocks exponential growth, a cascade of technological breakthroughs could spur unprecedented economic growth and expansion in military capabilities that some have termed agentic warfare. Under this scenario, an AGI-capable power could rapidly erode, if not eliminate, the second strike capabilities of a non-AGI power. This technological leap would amplify the unfortunate psychological tendency to become more risk-prone when facing losses, called prospect theory.

Accordingly, under AGI takeoff, non-AGI nuclear weapons powers, especially the weaker ones, will likely fear a near-future wherein they will be unable to deter the AGI power. They could therefore adopt a more aggressive posture. Of course, this isn’t the only rational reaction, but for reasons we will describe later, we think North Korea is much more likely to respond with extra aggression than it is to seek refuge through survivability, concealment, and arms control negotiations. Moreover, if recursive self-improvement delivers artificial superintelligence (ASI), defined as capabilities exceeding any human, the stakes will become much higher and nuclear decision-making timelines will become even more compressed.

AGI consequences, timelines, and diffusion remain a subject of debate, and key AI breakthroughs may be a business cycle or more away, but the balance of evidence suggests huge capability increases are possible. If scaling laws continue to hold, capabilities will keep rising: announced U.S. AI computing capacity is projected to increase by 239 percent this year alone, according to Federal Reserve staff calculations based on Epoch AI data. By 2030, planned U.S. AI compute would be roughly 35 times mid-2025 levels.

While tech CEOs and investors are incentivized to hype AI advances, models are undeniably improving, and at an impressive rate; the newest models are even proving adept at operating in the physical world. For better and for worse, AI software and hardware capabilities are advancing rapidly. Even artificial intelligence experts themselves have expressed surprise at the pace of innovation and warned of the dangers of unrestricted development.

Strategic deterrence nullification would likely lag AGI by many years, but AI timelines are advancing far faster than most expected. North Korea’s force posture is already changing and new command-and-control safeguards – including human-in-the-loop commitments – may take years to agree upon and implement.

AGI attainment would usher in considerable geopolitical disruptions, including altering the nuclear balance-of-power. China and Russia are of special importance in any AGI scenario. China is a peer competitor of the United States, including in AI, and it possesses the world’s third largest nuclear arsenal; Russia possesses the world’s largest nuclear weapon arsenal (by volume) and continues to face off against the United States in Cold War-style proxy conflict. Either competitor could be incentivized to act aggressively if the U.S. is first to approach AGI attainment.

Nevertheless, the gravest AGI-related dangers may come from less-capable nuclear powers, especially North Korea. That’s because Pyongyang has adopted a uniquely aggressive and decentralized form of nuclear command and control, has an aggressive nuclear doctrine, suffers from severe technical and even geographic disadvantages, and it maintains a paranoid disposition towards the United States. Faced with the prospect of losing second strike capability, it could therefore choose to adopt an even riskier posture or operationalize half-baked tech into its nuclear command, control, and communications before the United States crosses the AGI threshold.

Nuclear stability requires mutual vulnerability. China and Russia are more likely to continue to hold the U.S. hostage via threat of retaliation even if the U.S. obtains AGI first; for North Korea, that is much less likely.

AGI Takeoff, or Perceived Takeoff, Upends Conventional and Strategic Military Calculations

If AGI takeoff occurs, its technological, economic, and military consequences will be extremely hard to forecast. Physical constraints and hardware bottlenecks, including in critical minerals, could slow the transformation of software breakthroughs into weapons. Still, powerful AI could rapidly deliver unprecedented economic and technological capacity, which would then translate into military capabilities, including early warning, detection, targeting, and delivery. These capabilities could credibly threaten other states’ second-strike forces.

As the decision window shrinks, mutual vulnerability – the foundation of a stable deterrence relationship – will erode. Given the dangers of facing an AGI-empowered rival, and their own weak monitoring and verification capabilities, non-AGI powers like Pyongyang will watch anxiously for signs that an adversary’s AGI attainment could unlock the potential for a decapitation strike that wipes out their leadership and nuclear capabilities in one fell swoop.

In this scenario, facing rapidly deteriorating strategic options, a state could be motivated to automate nuclear retaliation. They might hope that the dead man’s hand would serve as a final guarantor of deterrence. But as human operators are pulled further out of the nuclear decision-making process, the ethical and practical problems will begin to multiply. History has proven that humans are the last best defense against needless escalation. That was the case in 1983 when a Soviet early warning system erroneously signaled an incoming U.S. intercontinental ballistic missile. Using his knowledge of the faulty system and U.S. strategy, Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov deduced that the warning was a false positive. He was right: the system’s satellites misread sunlight reflecting off clouds.

North Korea is thought to have a substantial inventory of both chemical and biological weapons, and it might lean on these capabilities if it fears its nuclear deterrent is compromised.
